title: House Takes Up Russia Sanctions Bill Named for Lindsey Graham
summary: The House voted Wednesday on a sweeping package of sanctions against Russia, named after the late Sen. Lindsey Graham of South Carolina, who spent over a year crafting it. The bill aims to cut off money for Russia's war in Ukraine by targeting Russian officials, banks, and a 'shadow fleet' of tankers that keeps Russian energy flowing. It also directs President Donald Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia's natural gas and have taken steps to reduce those imports. 'These countries have a choice to make about whether they will continue to sustain Putin's aggression,' said Rep. Michael McCaul, R-Texas. Supporters say the tariff threat is meant to deter China and India from buying Russian energy. But critics warn Trump could use it against European allies, and Americans would pay higher prices. 'This president has always said he loves tariffs,' said Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y. Democrats are divided. Rep. Steny Hoyer, D-Md., urged support: 'If we fail to pass this bill, there will be cheers in the Kremlin and tears in Kyiv.' But Rep. Don Beyer, D-Va., predicted regret, saying Trump might waive sanctions on Russia while hitting allies with tariffs. The bill represents the most ambitious effort to support Ukraine since Trump returned to office, breaking nearly two years of gridlock. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has pushed for its passage. If the House passes it, it goes to Trump's desk.
why_it_matters: Sanctions and tariffs are economic weapons, and votes like this one ripple outward — shaping the price of fuel and food, the strength of Russia's war effort, and whether the United States keeps its allies on its side.

background_read: The United States and its allies have been imposing sanctions on Russia since 2014, when Russia seized Crimea (a Ukrainian peninsula on the Black Sea), and then expanded them sharply after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Lindsey Graham (a U.S. senator from South Carolina who served in Congress for decades and was known for working across party lines on foreign policy) is the bill's namesake, and the article says he spent more than a year writing it.
Volodymyr Zelenskyy (Ukraine's president since 2019) has spent years asking Western governments for weapons, money and tougher measures against Moscow.
A 'shadow fleet' usually means tankers that are old, often uninsured, and sail with their tracking signals turned off so they can carry Russian oil past the price cap Western countries set on it.

The Kremlin (the Russian government, named after its walled compound in Moscow) argues that sanctions hurt the global economy, and Russia has redirected much of its oil to buyers in Asia, especially China and India.
Under the U.S. system, a bill must pass the House of Representatives and then the Senate before the president can sign it into law, which is why a House vote is only the first step.

perspectives.description: Backers like Rep. Michael McCaul argue the tariff threat forces countries such as China and India to choose between buying Russian energy and trading with the United States. They see the bill as the strongest bid to help Ukraine since Trump returned to office, which is why Zelenskyy has pushed for it.

Critics like Rep. Gregory Meeks warn that Trump 'loves tariffs' and could aim them at European allies instead of Russia, driving up prices for American consumers. Rep. Don Beyer fears a worst case where Trump waives sanctions on Russia while taxing friendly countries.

Sanctions have been a standard tool of U.S. foreign policy for decades, but combining them with tariffs aimed at third countries is unusual because it pressures allies and rivals at the same time. It also hands the president wide discretion over when to enforce or waive the measures.

If the House passes the bill, it still must clear the Senate and reach Trump's desk, where the waiver power means the real policy could end up looking different from the text. Both parties are already arguing about what that final version should contain.
